facts.claim: As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): the Marriage Act 1961 and the Marriage Regulations 2017 set the rules for getting married in Australia. AGD gives general guidance but not specific legal advice; for guidance ask AGD or an authorised marriage celebrant.

As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): to get married in Australia you must, among other things, 'give a notice of intended marriage form to an authorised marriage celebrant at least 1 month and no more than 18 months before your wedding' and 'be married by an authorised marriage celebrant'. The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): under 'Before you get married': 'complete a notice of intended marriage form' and 'give it to an authorised marriage celebrant at least 1 month (but not more than 18 months) before your wedding. Ask your authorised marriage celebrant if you need help with the form.' The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): 'You can complete it if you are overseas and plan to get married in Australia.'

As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): 'If there is less than 1 month until your wedding, talk to your authorised marriage celebrant. You may be able to get married if a prescribed authority approves it.' Reasons listed for getting married in less than 1 month: employment-related or travel commitments; wedding or celebration arrangements; medical reasons; legal proceedings; error in giving notice. The page links 'prescribed authority' to https://marriage.ag.gov.au/stateofficers/authorities (not read in this round). The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): 'Your authorised marriage celebrant will also need: evidence of your date and place of birth (birth certificate or passport); identity (driver's licence or passport); proof that a previous marriage has ended; to meet separately and in person with each party to a marriage.' The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): changes to the Marriage Act that became law on 12 June 2024: the option to have the NOIM witnessed remotely, via audio-visual link, as well as in person; an authorised celebrant must meet separately and in person with each party before the marriage is solemnised; re-ordering of the acceptable evidence of date and place of birth; clarifying that a NOIM can be transferred to another authorised celebrant, including at the request of the couple; clarifying that a celebrant must be physically present to solemnise a marriage, with the parties and 2 witnesses.

As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): 'The Notice of Intended Marriage form was updated on 1 September 2021.' The page links to the form download (https://www.ag.gov.au/node/3015) and other forms (https://www.ag.gov.au/node/1391).

As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): you don't have to be an Australian citizen or a permanent resident of Australia to marry in Australia; if you are not and want to live in Australia after marrying, find out about getting a visa (Home Affairs).

As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): to marry in Australia you must not be married; not be marrying a parent, grandparent, child, grandchild, brother or sister; be at least 18 (unless a court has approved a marriage where 1 person is 16 to 18); understand what marriage means and freely agree to marry; use specific words during the ceremony. 'The right to marry in Australia is no longer determined by sex or gender.'

As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): on the wedding day 3 marriage certificates must be signed by the couple, the authorised celebrant and 2 witnesses over 18. The celebrant gives the couple a ceremonial certificate of marriage on the day, then must, within 14 days of the marriage, submit the marriage paperwork to the registry of births, deaths and marriages in the state or territory where the marriage took place.

As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): 'You should apply for a copy of your official marriage certificate from the registry. Your celebrant can do this on your behalf, generally at a cost. You will need this if you want to change your name or prove that you are married.' (No amount stated.)

As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): overseas marriages cannot be performed by an Australian-authorised marriage celebrant and cannot be registered in Australia. An overseas marriage is generally recognised in Australia if it was a valid marriage in the overseas country and would have been a valid marriage here. Smartraveller has information on getting married overseas. The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): contact: Marriage Law and Celebrants Section, 1800 550 343; outside Australia +61 2 6141 3111; marriagecelebrantssection@ag.gov.au.

Marriage Act 1961 (Federal Register of Legislation, latest compilation dated 28 March 2026, read live 13 November 2026; table of contents only, section text not returned): Part IV Division 2 includes s 41 'Marriages to be solemnised by authorised celebrant', s 42 'Notice to be given and declaration made', s 42A 'Commissioner of Australian Federal Police or approved authority may issue special notice', s 42B 'Authorised celebrant must physically meet each party to intended marriage separately', s 44 'Witnesses', and s 104 'Giving defective notice etc.' (offence). The Act is administered by the Attorney-General's Department.

[Copied from is-marriage-in-italy-recognised-in-australia 03-source-pack fact_35, same source and date.] Attorney-General's Department, 'Get married': give the Notice of Intended Marriage to the authorised celebrant 'at least 1 month' and 'no more than 18 months' before the wedding; 'If there is less than 1 month until your wedding, talk to your authorised marriage celebrant. You may be able to get married if a prescribed authority approves it.' 'Your authorised marriage celebrant will also need to meet separately and in person with each party to a marriage' (changes from 12 June 2024).

[Copied from same-sex-marriage-greece 03-source-pack fact_106, same source and date.] As at November 2026, Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas' (last updated 18/08/2026, read live 12 November 2026): some countries ask you to prove you aren't already married; the most common documents are a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) and certificates from a registry of births, deaths and marriages; the country may have more rules (for example a residence period); 'We can't tell you what you will need'; contact your destination's embassy or consulate. The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

[Copied from same-sex-marriage-greece 03-source-pack fact_107, same source and date.] As at November 2026, Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas' (read live 12 November 2026): your registry of births, deaths and marriages can give a statement that there's no record you have been married before, a Single Status certificate or a No Record Result certificate; local authorities may also ask for divorce papers, the death certificate of a deceased spouse, and your original birth certificate and passport.

[Copied from same-sex-marriage-greece 03-source-pack fact_115 (originally mykonos-wedding part-1 fact_101), same source and date.] As at November 2026, Smartraveller (read live 11 November 2026) says DFAT can issue a CNI in Australia, but some local authorities only accept CNIs issued in their country, so ask the destination's embassy or consulate whether you need a CNI, whether you can get it in Australia, and whether it also needs an authentication or apostille. The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

[Copied from is-marriage-in-italy-recognised-in-australia 03-source-pack fact_01, same source and date.] Smartraveller (last updated Tuesday 18/08/2026): 'You can't register an overseas marriage in Australia. But in most cases, your marriage is legally recognised here. To be recognised, when you got married it must have been: valid under the law of the country where it happened; valid under Australian law if it had occurred in Australia.'

[Copied from is-marriage-in-italy-recognised-in-australia 03-source-pack fact_25, same source and date.] Smartraveller: 'A foreign marriage certificate is usually accepted as proof of the marriage. But you may be unable to use it as proof of a name change. Find out from your local registry of births, deaths and marriages.'

[Copied from is-marriage-in-italy-recognised-in-australia 03-source-pack fact_39, same source and date.] Attorney-General's Department, 'Marriage equality in Australia': 'If we recognise your marriage, you can't get married again in Australia. But you may choose to hold another type of ceremony, such as: confirmation of vows, recommitment ceremony.'

[Copied from is-marriage-in-italy-recognised-in-australia 03-source-pack fact_37, same source and date.] Marriage Act 1961 s 113(2) and (3): where there is a doubt whether the couple are legally married, whether an overseas marriage would be recognised as valid by an Australian court, or whether it could be proved in legal proceedings, they may marry again in Australia 'as if they had not previously gone through a form or ceremony of marriage'; they give the celebrant a statutory declaration of the earlier ceremony (date, place, circumstances) with a barrister's or solicitor's certificate endorsed on it that there is such a doubt.

facts.claim: [Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding 03-source-pack fact_319, same source and date.] Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: every Greek Orthodox Priest in Australia is also a registered civil celebrant, authorised to conduct the marriage under both State and Ecclesiastical law, but may perform the civil marriage only together with the religious service on the same day.

[Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding 03-source-pack fact_320, same source and date.] Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: the Notice of Intended Marriage (for the Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages) and the Application to the Archdiocese must be completed in the presence of the Priest at least one calendar month before the wedding, preferably three months. The Parish Priest gives directions on documents and on Archdiocese and local church fees, which vary by circumstances.

[Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding 03-source-pack fact_321, same source and date.] Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: both parties must present a birth certificate (if born in Australia) or passport (if born overseas) and a baptismal certificate; Orthodox parties never married before need a Certificate of Celibacy ('Agamias') from their local parish priest, signed by two witnesses. Widowed parties provide the spouse's death certificate.

The Attorney-General's Department's Notice of Intended Marriage publication page (last updated 22 December 2022) says section 42 of the Marriage Act 1961 requires that a marriage shall not be solemnised unless a notice in writing of the intended marriage (this form) is given to the authorised celebrant solemnising the marriage. The form is downloadable as PDF and DOCX.

AGD: from 12 June 2024 the Notice of Intended Marriage may be witnessed remotely; the Marriage Act was amended to permanently give couples the option of having the NOIM witnessed in person or remotely by a facility that enables audio and visual communication between people in different places.

AGD: the requirements for authorised witnesses remain unchanged and location-dependent. If the couple is in Australia, the person remotely witnessing the NOIM (which can include an authorised celebrant) must also be in Australia. If the couple is outside Australia, the authorised witness (which cannot be a celebrant) must also be outside Australia. A NOIM for a person or couple outside Australia cannot be witnessed online.
AGD: authorised witnesses are listed in the 'Signatures of parties and witnesses' section of the Notice of Intended Marriage form.

The Attorney-General's Department's list of prescribed authorities says a prescribed authority is an officer or employee of the Commonwealth, a State or Territory appointed by the Attorney-General, and is authorised, among other things, to authorise a marriage celebrant to proceed with a marriage ceremony where the minimum one-month notice has not been provided (shortening of time). The list is searchable by state and territory and includes registrars and deputy registrars of local courts and state registries of births, deaths and marriages.

insider_details.detail: For an Australian ceremony the NOIM window is at least 1 month and no more than 18 months before the date, so couples planning a long engagement should lodge once the date and celebrant are locked, not before the 18-month mark.

Couples living overseas can still complete the NOIM before flying home to marry in Australia, and since 12 June 2024 it can be witnessed by audio-visual link as well as in person, but the celebrant must still meet each partner separately and in person before the wedding, so build that meeting into the arrival schedule.

A NOIM is only needed for a marriage solemnised in Australia. A destination wedding abroad cannot be performed by an Australian celebrant or registered here; the paperwork instead runs through the destination's own requirements, often a CNI, which DFAT can issue but some countries only accept if issued locally.

Couples who legally marry abroad cannot then lodge a NOIM and marry again in Australia if the overseas marriage is recognised; a home celebration becomes a vow renewal or recommitment ceremony instead.
For a Greek Orthodox wedding in Australia the priest is also the civil celebrant, so the NOIM is signed with the priest; the Archdiocese asks for at least one calendar month and preferably three.

Order documents early: the celebrant needs evidence of date and place of birth, identity and proof any earlier marriage has ended. Divorce or death certificates for a previous spouse are the slowest to locate, especially from overseas registries.
